items.definition: A body of ideas about how conflict works, built from the study of past campaigns rather than from rules of fighting.
items.example: The book is called a theory of war because it explains how conflict works, not how to fight.

items.definition: The Prussian officer (1780-1831) who wrote On War, the book that gave the field its central sentence.
items.example: Clausewitz wrote that war is the continuation of politics by other means.

items.definition: The business of running a state and its relations with other states; in the theory of war, the purpose that fighting is meant to serve.
items.example: The war had a political purpose, so the settlement had to satisfy the politics.

items.definition: The way a conflict is linked to its political purpose: what is wanted, with what means, over what time.
items.example: The strategy of the campaign was to hold the coast and wait.

items.definition: The level between strategy and tactics: the way a whole campaign is carried out, across a front, week by week.
items.example: The operations ran out of fuel before the plan reached its objective.

items.definition: The level of the local action: how a unit is used in one fight and how it is moved on the field.
items.example: The report describes tactics when it explains how the advance was carried out.

items.definition: A series of connected actions with one objective, from the first move to the decision that closes it.
items.example: The campaign lasted six weeks and ended at the river.

items.definition: Strategy at the level of a whole state: how a country uses its power over years to reach a political aim.
items.example: Containment was the grand strategy, and deterrence was one of its tools.

items.definition: The result a plan aims at, written so that it can be judged done or not done.
items.example: The brief states the objective in one line: the river crossing.

items.definition: The directions from which an attack may come, and the ground they must cross.
items.example: The lines of approach were limited by the marsh.

items.definition: The place or the moment where the outcome of the whole action is settled; the effort is concentrated there.
items.example: The decisive point was the bridge, and the plan said so.

items.definition: Means held back from the first effort and kept for the moment the situation turns.
items.example: The plan kept one reserve for the second week.

items.definition: The routes along which orders, reports and supplies travel to the fighting units.
items.example: The lines of communication were cut by the flood.

items.definition: The small resistance between wanting something and getting it, which slows consumption and quietly trains patience.
items.example: Every plan met friction: the weather, the delay, the wrong order.

items.definition: The state of not knowing: incomplete reports, false information and the general uncertainty of events.
items.example: In the fog of war the commander acted on a report three days old.

items.definition: Taking a matter to a more senior person because it has not moved. Use it only when it is genuinely warranted.
items.example: If we do not hear back by Friday, we will need to escalate this.

items.definition: The ladder of steps a conflict can climb, from a limited incident up to a general war.
items.example: Analysts place the crisis three rungs up the escalation ladder.

items.definition: The effort to prevent an opponent's action by making the cost of it too high.
items.example: Deterrence holds only if the opponent believes both the ability and the will.

items.definition: The case where the opponent acts anyway: the threat was not believed, or it was believed and the cost was accepted.
items.example: Deterrence failure means the action went ahead anyway.

items.definition: A threat that is made without the means or the intention to carry it out.
items.example: A threat made without the means to carry it out is a bluff, and it costs nothing to make.

items.definition: A conflict between opponents whose resources, organisation and methods differ greatly.
items.example: The article calls it an asymmetric conflict and says where the difference lies.

items.definition: The wearing down of the opponent by continued cost, rather than by one decisive stroke.
items.example: Attrition decided the campaign; no single battle did.

items.definition: The line where the two sides stand against each other, and the whole stretch of fighting behind it.
items.example: The front held for three months while both sides rebuilt.

items.definition: The side that attacks; in the phrase the offensive, the direction of the action.
items.example: The offensive stopped when the supplies ran out.

items.definition: The side that receives the attack and holds ground; the opposite of the offensive.
items.example: A defensive plan is judged by the ground it gives up.

items.definition: The work of moving and supplying the fighting: food, fuel, ammunition, vehicles and spares.
items.example: The report says the problem was logistics, not the fighting.

items.definition: The spirit and the confidence of a force; the strength it holds when things go badly.
items.example: Morale fell as the third convoy did not arrive.
